title: Indices

findings.finding: Negative bases are required before teaching distinguishes a signed base from a minus sign outside a power.
findings.breakdown: Students may treat −3² and (−3)² alike. Positive-base examples do not expose this distinction, and the comparison in p14-q10 follows the first required negative-base evaluations.
findings.checked: The index definitions, expanded-form examples and p10 examples use positive bases. The order-of-operations chart does not explicitly identify the base of a signed power.
findings.assumptions: Signed multiplication is prior knowledge; applying index notation to signed bases is new here. Calculator access does not resolve the notation.

repair.proposal: Before p14-q7-d add: “Brackets make the whole signed number the base: (−3)²=(−3)×(−3)=9 and (−3)³=(−3)×(−3)×(−3)=−27. Without brackets, −3²=−(3×3)=−9.”

findings.doneWhen: The signed-base distinction is explicitly modelled before its first required use.

findings.finding: A fixed-units-digit run can distinguish divisibility by 4 from merely being even.
findings.breakdown: Changing only the tens digit makes divisibility alternate while every number remains even.
findings.checked: The divisibility tests supply the necessary method. The existing question has no comparable consecutive run. All proposed classifications are correct.
findings.assumptions: Students use the existing instruction to circle multiples of 4.

repair.proposal: Append: “Predict which numbers you will circle.” Add m) 112, n) 122, o) 132, p) 142, followed by unpatterned q) 276. Circle 112, 132 and 276; do not circle 122 or 142. Across m–p only the tens digit changes.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run follows p17-q2-l under the existing instruction.

findings.finding: The square-root model introduces 14 without showing the regrouping that produces it.
findings.breakdown: The rule 'multiply each distinct prime once' succeeds throughout question 9 but fails when question 10 contains several pairs of the same prime.
findings.checked: p30-q17 demonstrates distributing a power across a product, but does not model selecting factors from repeated pairs for a root. p36-q9-a jumps from 2^2×7^2 to 14^2; subsequent scaffolded examples retain the special case of one pair per prime.
findings.assumptions: Students know prime factorisation and repeated multiplication. Calculator access does not model the grouping decision.

repair.proposal: Add to p36-q9-a: 'Regroup into two identical products: 2×2×7×7=(2×7)×(2×7)=14^2. For the square root, take one factor from every pair, including each repeated pair of the same prime.'

findings.doneWhen: The model shows where 14 comes from and explicitly retains one factor from every pair.

findings.finding: Extend the existing root calculation to products with square factors.
findings.breakdown: Students connect an added pair of equal factors with a multiplier outside the root.
findings.checked: Using 784=28² gives √(784×9)=84 and √(784×25)=140. Repeated factors and inverse squaring suffice.
findings.assumptions: Use positive square roots and the factorisation already obtained in Question 11.

repair.proposal: After p36-q11-b-root add optional parts: (c) Using √784=28, find √(784×9) without a calculator. Answer: 84. (d) Find √(784×25). Answer: 140. (e) Explain why multiplying 784 by 9 multiplies its square root by 3. Answer: 9=3² supplies one additional pair of factors 3, contributing one factor 3 to the root.

findings.doneWhen: The extension appears as further parts of Question 11, with one question per part.

findings.finding: Fourth- and fifth-root notation appears before its meaning is supplied.
findings.breakdown: Knowing square and cube roots does not establish what the new small indices ask students to undo.
findings.checked: p33 and p38 define square and cube roots only. p40-q5 supplies higher-root inverse relationships later, after p40-q4.
findings.assumptions: Higher-root notation is new within this booklet. A calculator is available as explicitly permitted by p40-q4.

repair.proposal: Before p40-q4, add: 'The small root index tells us which power to undo. For positive numbers and a positive integer n, √[n]{a}=b means b^n=a. For example, 3^4=81, so √[4]{81}=3.'

findings.doneWhen: The root index’s meaning and an explicit inverse pair precede fourth- and fifth-root evaluation.

findings.finding: Use the supplied cubes to connect doubling an edge with an eightfold cube count.
findings.breakdown: The extension links the three factors in cubing to a concrete change in the existing diagrams.
findings.checked: Parts a–c contain 8, 27 and 64 cubes. Doubling the three-block edge gives 6³=216, which is eight times 27. All required methods are already available.
findings.assumptions: The small cubes have equal dimensions.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (d) The cube in c has twice as many blocks along each edge as the cube in a. How many times as many small cubes does it contain? Answer: 64÷8=8. (e) Double the number of blocks along each edge of the cube in b. How many small cubes would the new cube contain? Answer: 6³=216. (f) How many times the original 27 cubes is this? Answer: 216÷27=8.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up appears as further parts of p39-q2.

findings.finding: The independent exercise repeats the complete guided task √(3^2+4^2).
findings.breakdown: Both ask for evaluation of the unchanged expression.
findings.checked: Compared the expression and parent instructions. Neither states a retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.assumptions: The supplied instructions contain the complete student-facing purpose.

repair.proposal: Remove p44-q1-g.

findings.doneWhen: The unchanged task appears once in this sequence.

findings.finding: The symbolic different-base quotient needs a grouping route that the same-base division teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: Students are correctly taught to reject index subtraction for different bases, but must now form repeated copies of m/p to obtain the expected index-form result.
findings.checked: p30-q17 supplies product grouping, not quotient grouping. p50 identifies different bases as outside the division law; preceding parts reinforce that restriction.
findings.assumptions: Students know positive-power expansion and ordinary fraction multiplication. The denominator p is nonzero.

repair.proposal: Append: 'The bases differ, so do not subtract indices. Expand m^4/p^4, then group it as (m/p)×(m/p)×(m/p)×(m/p). Write this product in index form.'

findings.doneWhen: The question supplies the grouping route and distinguishes it from same-base index subtraction.

findings.finding: The exercise requires the booklet's treatment of 0⁰ without stating it.
findings.breakdown: Excluding zero from a⁰=1 establishes that the rule cannot be applied, but does not establish the requested classification as undefined.
findings.checked: The sequences and division demonstrations use nonzero bases. The complete earlier teaching does not state a convention for 0⁰.
findings.assumptions: The intended school-arithmetic convention is the supplied answer, undefined.

repair.proposal: After p55-zero-power-rule add: “The zero-index rule applies only to nonzero bases. In this booklet, 0⁰ is treated as undefined.”

findings.doneWhen: The convention is stated before p56-q1-m.

findings.finding: The opening example uses division-before-addition recall without rehearsing it.
findings.breakdown: Students must keep the separate addend outside the quotient while applying the division index law.
findings.checked: p10 teaches operation order. p57’s review rehearses individual index laws, not choosing between addition and division. The supplied preceding mixed-practice task does not rehearse that choice.
findings.assumptions: Operation order is previously taught but may need retrieval. Calculator access does not remove the decision.

repair.proposal: Before p64-example, ask: 'Evaluate using the order of operations: (a) 6+12÷3; (b) 3+2^3×2; (c) (3+2^3)×2.' Answers: 10, 19, 22.

findings.doneWhen: A short review rehearses a separate addend, power priority and grouping.

findings.finding: Mixed composite-base powers require a product-power relationship that earlier teaching has not established for these powers.
findings.breakdown: Same-base laws and power of a power do not explain splitting 15⁹⁹⁹ into 5⁹⁹⁹×3⁹⁹⁹ or applying a composite base's exponent to each prime factor.
findings.checked: The complete index-law teaching lists multiplication, division, nested powers and zero power. p36-q9 supplies numerical square-product instances, but no teaching connects repeated composite factors to distributing an arbitrary positive integer power.
findings.assumptions: This relationship has not been separately taught. Calculator evaluation cannot replace the intended index-law reasoning.

repair.proposal: Before p68-q11-b add: “(2×3)³=(2×3)(2×3)(2×3)=(2×2×2)(3×3×3)=2³×3³. A positive whole-number power of a product raises each factor to that power: each repeated product contributes one copy of every factor.” Then cue: “Write 15 as 5×3 before applying this relationship.”

findings.doneWhen: A repeated-factor demonstration establishes the product-power step before its first use and supports the later prime-power tasks.

findings.finding: Extend the existing nested power by comparing multiplication by 2 with squaring.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up distinguishes adding one to an index from doubling the index.
findings.checked: (2³)⁴=2¹². Multiplication by 2 gives 2¹³, squaring gives 2²⁴, and the multiplier connecting 2¹² to 2²⁴ is 2¹². All methods are taught.
findings.assumptions: Answers remain in index form.

repair.proposal: After existing part c append optional parts: (d) Write (2³)⁴×2 as a single power of 2. Answer: 2¹³. (e) Write ((2³)⁴)² as a single power of 2. Answer: 2²⁴. (f) What power of 2 must multiply (2³)⁴ to give ((2³)⁴)²? Answer: 2¹².

findings.doneWhen: The three numerical follow-up parts appear under Question 13.

findings.finding: The HCF method uses prime factorisation in index form without an opening rehearsal.
findings.breakdown: Students need to produce complete prime factorisations before selecting minimum or maximum indices.
findings.checked: p23–p24 teach factorisation and compression. The immediately preceding topic practises evaluating index expressions rather than constructing prime factorisations. p69 demonstrates calculator access to a factorisation but provides no retrieval task.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are available as stated in p69. The review concerns producing and interpreting factorisations, not evaluating powers or products.

repair.proposal: Before p69-dot-operator, ask: 'Write each number as a product of prime factors in index form. Use a factor tree if helpful: (a) 28; (b) 45; (c) 72.' Answers: 2^2×7; 3^2×5; 2^3×3^2.

findings.doneWhen: Students briefly rehearse complete prime factorisations in index form before the HCF example.

findings.finding: The factor-counting tasks require an unexplained connection between prime-exponent choices and all factors.
findings.breakdown: Students must identify the allowed exponents, include zero and combine independent choices. Earlier factorisation and zero-index teaching do not establish this counting method.
findings.checked: p76-q8-a supplies factorisation preparation, but no preceding instruction connects exponent combinations to counting factors. p76-q9 adds a third prime before modelling that connection.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary factor lists are prior knowledge; counting factors through exponent choices is new.

repair.proposal: Append to p76-q8-b: “Every factor is 2ᵃ×3ᵇ. List the possible values of a and b, including zero. Make a table with one row for each possible a and one column for each possible b, and put the corresponding factor in each cell. How many cells are there?” Expected choices: a=0,1,2 and b=0,1,2,3, giving 12 cells.

findings.doneWhen: The first task exposes the exponent choices and their combinations before the three-prime task.

findings.finding: The general HCF–LCM product explanation precedes the existing numerical investigation that prepares it.
findings.breakdown: p77-q15 moves from calculating HCFs and LCMs to relating their products and explaining the prime-index mechanism at once. p80-q33 already separates these demands.
findings.checked: The HCF and LCM teaching supplies minimum and maximum indices but does not compare the two products. p80-q33 explicitly supplies factorisation, calculation, comparison and explanation in stages.
findings.assumptions: The product relationship has not been established separately.

repair.proposal: Move p80-q33 immediately before p77-q15, preserving all its parts.

findings.doneWhen: The concrete product comparison precedes the general explanation.

findings.finding: Counting integers divisible by neither number introduces overlapping exclusions without exposing the double subtraction.
findings.breakdown: Subtracting multiples of both 5 and 7 removes the ten multiples of 35 twice. Part a rehearses only a single exclusion.
findings.checked: Earlier divisibility and LCM tasks identify common multiples but do not connect them to correcting overlapping counts. The preceding part does not reveal the overlap.
findings.assumptions: Overlapping-set counting has not already been taught separately; counting multiples is available.

repair.proposal: Append: “If you subtract both the multiples of 5 and the multiples of 7, which numbers have you subtracted twice? Use their LCM to count these numbers and add that count back once.” The resulting count is 350−70−50+10=240.

findings.doneWhen: The first overlapping-exclusion task prompts students to identify and correct the double subtraction.

findings.finding: Questions requiring all inverse HCF–LCM pairs precede the existing structured reconstruction.
findings.breakdown: Students must reconstruct numbers satisfying both constraints and establish that the pairs are complete. p89-q67 separates the common factor, coprime residual factors and their product.
findings.checked: In the supplied practice order, p89-q68 and p89-q69 precede p89-q67. p95-q87 is excluded from the finding: it asks only for a possible pair, and the given HCF and LCM themselves supply one.
findings.assumptions: The coprime-factor reconstruction method has not been taught separately.

repair.proposal: Move p89-q67 immediately before p89-q68, preserving its complete sequence of parts.

findings.doneWhen: The structured reconstruction precedes both tasks requiring the possible pairs.

findings.finding: Parts d and e repeat the same whole task.
findings.breakdown: Both supply the prefix 21 and request two final digits making the number divisible by 5.
findings.checked: Compared the shared instruction, prefixes and response requirements. No comparison or retrieval purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: The supplied prompts are complete.

repair.proposal: Remove p17-q3-e.

findings.doneWhen: The unchanged 21-prefix task appears once.

findings.finding: Students are asked to classify a thirteen-digit number without a feasible supplied method for establishing its primality.
findings.breakdown: Failing the six taught divisibility tests does not establish primality. The instruction to use these tests risks students treating their failure as proof.
findings.checked: p16-tests covers only 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. p22 supplies definitions, small arrays and the first ten primes. The teacher-supplied classification appears only in the answer.
findings.assumptions: An ordinary calculator may be available; no primality-testing facility is assumed. Practice answers are not student-facing teaching.

repair.proposal: Label k: 'Teacher discussion: your teacher will supply this number’s classification. Explain why failing the divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 does not prove that a number is prime.'

findings.doneWhen: The student-facing task identifies the teacher-supplied classification and asks students to explain the tests’ limitation.

findings.finding: The factor-tree example uses mixed-factor compression into index form without an opening rehearsal.
findings.breakdown: Students must count repeated prime factors and retain single factors to connect the tree’s leaves to 2^3 × 5.
findings.checked: p3-rewrite teaches this skill. The immediately preceding prime-number teaching rehearses classification, not index compression. p23-identify requests prime products without rehearsing their compression.
findings.assumptions: Previously taught index notation needs retrieval here. Calculator availability does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Before p23-theorem-block, ask: 'Write in index form: (a) 2×2×2; (b) 3×3×5; (c) 5×2×5×2×2.' Answers: 2^3; 3^2×5; 2^3×5^2.

findings.doneWhen: A short review rehearses repeated-factor counting, single factors and mixed-factor grouping before the example.

findings.finding: Question 2 contains unchanged repeated tasks for √49 and √169.
findings.breakdown: Each later copy repeats the complete expression and evaluation requirement.
findings.checked: Compared all four prompts under the same Evaluate instruction. No comparison or retrieval purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: These are separate student tasks.

repair.proposal: Remove p34-q2-k and p34-q2-m.

findings.doneWhen: Each targeted root appears once within question 2.

findings.finding: Generalise the prime-factor pairing condition for a perfect square.
findings.breakdown: The task connects root extraction to even prime multiplicities.
findings.checked: The first and third proposed products are squares; the second contains an unpaired factor 2. Factorisation, indices and square roots are available by the topic’s end.
findings.assumptions: The general rule concerns positive integers greater than 1.

repair.proposal: After p36-q12-c, offer: 'Without evaluating, which are perfect squares: 2^4×3^2, 2^3×3^2, and 2^2×3^4×5^2? Explain and state a rule.' Expected answer: the first and third; a positive integer greater than 1 is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task includes the products, explanation prompt and expected rule.

findings.finding: The cube-root estimation task does not identify how to adapt the taught square-root bounds.
findings.breakdown: Students must choose neighbouring perfect cubes and convert them into cube-root bounds; preceding estimation teaching specifies perfect squares only.
findings.checked: p38 establishes exact cubes and cube roots. p41-estimating-method, its example and guided questions model square-root bounds exclusively.
findings.assumptions: Calculator checking is available, but the task asks students to estimate.

repair.proposal: Before p42-q3, add: 'For cube roots, use neighbouring perfect cubes. For example, 27<40<64, so 3<∛40<4. Then check with a calculator: ∛40≈3.42.'

findings.doneWhen: A short cue connects neighbouring cubes to root bounds before independent cube-root estimates.

findings.finding: The root-expression examples use index priority and grouping without an opening rehearsal of operation order.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall powers before subtraction and complete grouped calculations while learning the scope of a root.
findings.checked: p10 teaches these decisions. The immediately preceding root-estimation review and exercise do not rehearse mixed-operation order. p43 restates the hierarchy but supplies no retrieval questions.
findings.assumptions: Calculator access does not remove the need to choose operation order.

repair.proposal: Before p43-order, ask: 'Evaluate using the order of operations. Write your first calculation on a new line: (a) 3^2−4; (b) (2+3)^2; (c) 18÷3^2+1.' Answers: 5, 25, 3.

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review rehearses index priority and grouping before roots are incorporated.

findings.finding: Explain why square roots split across products of positive perfect squares but generally not across sums.
findings.breakdown: The task develops the equality already encountered in question 2 and exposes an invalid addition rule.
findings.checked: The product expressions both equal 12; the sum expressions equal 5 and 7. Repeated multiplication and inverse squaring suffice for the stated domain.
findings.assumptions: The generalisation is restricted to positive perfect squares.

repair.proposal: After p45-q2, offer: 'Compare √(9×16) with √9×√16, and √(9+16) with √9+√16. Which equality holds for every pair of positive perfect squares? Explain.' Expected answer: the product pair both equal 12; the sum pair equal 5 and 7. If the squares are m^2 and n^2 with positive integer m,n, their product is (mn)^2, whose square root is mn.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task includes the product/sum comparison and an explanation within the stated domain.

findings.finding: The introductory calculations do not distinguish ordered index subtraction from taking a positive difference.
findings.breakdown: Subtracting the smaller index from the larger succeeds in every introductory calculation but incorrectly gives 5^4 for the reversed quotient.
findings.checked: p50-investigation, p50-simplify and p51-q1–q2 use larger numerator indices. The reversed applicability example identifies the law without calculating; the general formula alone does not expose the wrong rule.
findings.assumptions: This finding concerns subtraction order, independently of whether negative-index meanings were taught elsewhere. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p51-q3-05, add: 'Order matters: 5^6÷5^2=5^(6−2)=5^4, whereas 5^2÷5^6=5^(2−6)=5^(−4). Subtract the denominator’s index from the numerator’s index.'

findings.doneWhen: An explicit reversed contrast distinguishes ordered subtraction from a positive difference.

findings.finding: Question 3 repeats two unchanged whole tasks.
findings.breakdown: Parts 13 and 20 both request simplification of 4^0.6/4^0.2; parts 15 and 21 both request simplification of 4^6/4^6.
findings.checked: Compared complete expressions under the shared instruction. No additional givens, diagrams or explicit repetition purpose distinguishes the later copies.
findings.assumptions: No unstated retrieval purpose is assumed.

repair.proposal: Remove p51-q3-20 and p51-q3-21. Retain p51-q3-13 in its integer/decimal/fractional comparison and p51-q3-15 beside its symbolic generalisation.

findings.doneWhen: Each targeted task appears once and the earlier variation groups remain intact.

findings.finding: The task requires the booklet’s treatment of 0^0 without stating it.
findings.breakdown: Excluding zero from a^0=1 tells students that the rule cannot be applied, but does not supply the requested classification of 0^0.
findings.checked: p55 consistently restricts the zero-power rule and division argument to nonzero bases. Positive powers of zero in p56 do not establish the treatment of 0^0.
findings.assumptions: The expected answer uses the school convention that 0^0 is undefined.

repair.proposal: Add to p55-zero-power-rule: 'In this booklet, 0^0 is left undefined. The division argument cannot determine it because division by zero is undefined.'

findings.doneWhen: The booklet explicitly states its treatment of 0^0 before asking students to classify it.

findings.finding: The exercises repeat unchanged evaluation tasks for (5^6)^0 and 4^0.
findings.breakdown: Each later copy has the same expression, givens and evaluation requirement as its earlier copy.
findings.checked: Compared complete prompts and parent instructions. Neither repeated task has a stated retrieval or comparison purpose; removing these standalone parts preserves the shared stems.
findings.assumptions: An unstated repetition purpose is not assumed.

repair.proposal: Remove p65-q2-l and p65-q3-j.

findings.doneWhen: The unnecessary later copies are removed.

findings.finding: Common-base practice combines several new decisions before the existing preparation is encountered.
findings.breakdown: p68-q10-b adds independent base conversion, conversion inside a powered base, power-of-a-power simplification and combination of three factors after one supplied substitution.
findings.checked: Read the supplied practice order. p67-q7 provides common-base product rewriting, p67-q8 models a powered converted base, and p67-q9 scaffolds combined quotients, but all appear after p68-q10.
findings.assumptions: The supplied practice order is booklet order. Individual index laws and prime factorisation are already taught.

repair.proposal: Move p67-q7-block, p67-q8-block and p67-q9-block, in that order, immediately before p68-q10. Include the same-base equation cue from the merged unknown-index finding before p67-q8-c.

findings.doneWhen: The existing preparation precedes the combined common-base tasks.

findings.finding: Unknown-index tasks require the connection from equal powers to equal indices without a supplied model.
findings.breakdown: Students can rewrite both sides with a common base yet lack a demonstrated route from that equality to an equation in the indices.
findings.checked: p52 teaches multiplying nested indices. p68-q13 compares known powers. The earlier p62-q15 also requires an exponent inference but supplies no student-facing method. None models solving an unknown-index equation.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary linear-equation solving is prior knowledge. The relevant bases are positive and greater than 1.

repair.proposal: Before the first unknown-index task, add: 'Once both sides are powers of the same base here, set their indices equal and solve. For example, 2^(3t)=2^12 gives 3t=12, so t=4.' With the proposed reorder, place this before p67-q8-c.

findings.doneWhen: A written model connects equal powers to an equation in their indices before the affected tasks.

findings.finding: Vary one prime index across the point where the minimum and maximum change.
findings.breakdown: The run makes the different effects on HCF and LCM visible.
findings.checked: The proposed HCF/LCM pairs are (18,72), (36,72), (72,72), (72,144). The unpatterned pair has HCF 6 and LCM 1260. All methods are taught by p71.
findings.assumptions: All numbers are positive integers.

repair.proposal: After p71-guided, fix A=2^3·3^2. For B=2^1·3^2, 2^2·3^2, 2^3·3^2 and 2^4·3^2, predict before calculating which of HCF and LCM changes from the preceding pair, then find both. Only B’s index of 2 varies. Expected pairs: (18,72), (36,72), (72,72), (72,144). Follow with A=2^2·3·5 and B=2·3^2·7; expected HCF 6, LCM 1260.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run includes prediction, four single-feature variations and an unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: Explain the HCF–LCM product identity and why it does not extend directly to three numbers.
findings.breakdown: Students connect minimum and maximum prime indices to the multiplication law.
findings.checked: For two indices, minimum plus maximum equals their sum. For 2,4,8, HCF×LCM=16 while the three-number product is 64. All required methods are available.
findings.assumptions: The task concerns positive integers.

repair.proposal: After p73-q2-c, offer: 'For positive integers a,b, explain using prime factorisations why HCF(a,b)·LCM(a,b)=ab. Does HCF(a,b,c)·LCM(a,b,c)=abc always hold? Test 2,4,8 and explain.' Expected answer: minimum and maximum indices sum to the original two indices; for three numbers they omit the middle index. The example gives 16 rather than 64.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task states the positive-integer domain and includes the counterexample and structural explanation.

findings.finding: The unscaffolded least-divisor square task precedes the existing multiplication-to-division bridge.
findings.breakdown: p78-q24 combines factorisation, selecting factors to remove and establishing leastness before students encounter the scaffolded division variant.
findings.checked: In the supplied practice order, p77-q20 and p78-q21 also appear after p78-q24. p78-q22 supplies factorisation followed by matched multiplication and division tasks; p78-q23 then repeats that structure.
findings.assumptions: The supplied practice order is booklet order. Earlier square-root factorisation is available; no separate root-factorisation repair is required.

repair.proposal: Move p78-q24 to immediately after p78-q22, retaining p77-q20 and p78-q21 before p78-q22.

findings.doneWhen: Square-completing multiplication and the scaffolded division variant precede the unscaffolded 3060/n task.

protectedGroups.varies: Number length and place values: 108 becomes 10 800.
protectedGroups.invariant: Nonzero digits, digit sum and divisibility by 3.

protectedGroups.varies: Direction of implication, followed by the factor pair.
protectedGroups.invariant: The target number 24 and the relationship between divisibility conditions.
